title: How John Rush generates startup ideas: pain mining, keywords, clones and one-feature micro-SaaS
summary: John Rush walks through his methods for finding startup ideas: replying to public complaints with a solution, tweeting many ideas, cloning across markets, keyword research, automating your own job, and splitting out one feature of a big tool. He argues for starting with safe, simple ideas, being patient, and building for trends before they get big.

principles.text: Prefer B2B pain over B2C: businesses change habits to make more money, consumers rarely change habits.
principles.quote: with b2v it's easier because it's money if you use better tools you make more profits that's why people are more likely to change their habits

principles.text: Find a pain people complain about publicly, offer a solution on the spot, and validate with a waitlist before building.
principles.quote: single best way to find an idea is to see that people complain about something and then offer solution right there so that you validate whether the person who complaints thinks it's a good solution

principles.text: Pitch many ideas publicly; most flop unseen, and a hit with no followers proves the idea is good.
principles.quote: if you have chance to try 50 ideas just be by like one of them will be good you don't know which one and that's why you should try to pitch your idea to the market

principles.text: Start with safe ideas: clone a proven product into a new market, or change its price or audience. Skip the romantic world-changer story.
principles.quote: when you start you should remove the Romantic po of you being next to jobs changing the world at least for the first idea

principles.text: Take one feature of a big tool, build a micro-SaaS for only that, cheaper, with an obvious keyword name. It is validated, SEO-friendly and easy to recommend.
principles.quote: you take that feature and you build a tool a micros house with one feature all day you you don't add anything else only that one feature and then you drop the price

principles.text: Work on things of tomorrow: pick an area you know deeply, predict where it goes, and build before the wave is big.
principles.quote: you should always work on things of tomorrow okay so you should always try to predict because it takes time for you to gain experience
